differential: English has no equivalent; 'enjoyment' loses the transgressive dimension and the beyond-the-pleasure-principle connotation. Anglophone Lacanian literature retains the French term precisely because jouissance names the painful-pleasurable excess that 'enjoyment' domesticates. The legal sense (right of use/possession) active in French is also lost

The French signifiant is a present participle (that which signifies), preserving the active processual sense from Saussure. English 'signifier' is a nominalised agent-noun that fixes the concept into a static entity. Lacan's formula 'un signifiant représente le sujet pour un autre signifiant' exploits the participial dynamism that English flattens

French signifié is a past participle (that which has been signified), marking it as an effect of signification. English 'signified' preserves this grammatical structure adequately, making this one of the less problematic translations in the Saussurean-Lacanian lexicon

French distinguishes savoir (know-how, articulated knowledge, the knowledge of the unconscious in Lacan) from connaissance (acquaintance, imaginary knowledge, ego-knowledge). English collapses both into 'knowledge', destroying a distinction Lacan treats as fundamental: savoir is symbolic, connaissance is imaginary

Connaissance designates the ego's imaginary self-knowledge (méconnaissance = mis-recognition is its negative). English 'knowledge' cannot mark this as distinct from savoir. Some translators use 'acquaintance' or 'cognizance' but neither has gained standard acceptance, leaving English readers unable to hear Lacan's savoir/connaissance opposition

French pouvoir functions simultaneously as noun (power) and verb (to be able to, can). Foucault exploits this ambiguity: pouvoir is not a substance possessed but an ability exercised — 'power' in English is predominantly nominal, losing the verbal-modal dimension that makes Foucault's analytics of power irreducible to a theory of domination

In Saussure, parole (individual speech act) opposes langue (language system). Lacan's parole pleine (full speech) vs parole vide (empty speech) exploits connotations of parole as given word, promise, and oath — English 'speech' loses these juridical and performative resonances. 'Word' would capture the oath-dimension but lose the Saussurean technical sense

French distinguishes langue (language as formal system, Saussure's sense) from langage (the general human capacity for language). English 'language' covers both indiscriminately. When Lacan says 'l'inconscient est structuré comme un langage', the choice of langage over langue is theoretically significant but invisible in the standard English translation

Langage designates the general faculty or dimension of language (broader than any particular langue). English 'language' cannot mark the distinction from langue, collapsing two levels — the capacity and the system — into one word. Some translators italicize or bracket the French to signal the difference

Derrida's neologism replaces the 'e' of différence with 'a' — a substitution audible only in writing (French pronunciation is identical). English retains the French term because 'differance' would lose the specifically French homophony between différence and différance that is the concept's point: the difference that cannot be heard, only written

Standard French différence translates straightforwardly to 'difference'. The translation problem arises only in relation to différance: English 'difference' adequately renders différence, but the near-identity between différence and différance that Derrida exploits has no English parallel — English spelling and pronunciation both distinguish 'difference' from 'differance'

The French term preserves the morphological transparency of dé-territoire-isation (un-territory-ization) that English 'deterritorialization' also preserves reasonably well. The main translation issue is not semantic but pragmatic: French allows the verb déterritorialiser and its reflexive se déterritorialiser naturally, while English 'to deterritorialize' remains awkward and marked as jargon

Pairs with déterritorialisation as its dialectical complement. English 'reterritorialization' is morphologically transparent and semantically adequate. The translation difficulty is contextual: Deleuze-Guattari use the pair as a single conceptual machine (every deterritorialization accompanied by reterritorialization), and this paired usage survives translation intact

Massumi chose 'assemblage' for agencement, but the French term derives from agencer (to arrange, to lay out) and carries connotations of agency (agent) absent in 'assemblage' which suggests a static collection of parts. Agencement emphasizes the active arrangement and the capacity to act; 'assemblage' has become standard but systematically obscures the agentive dimension

Foucault's dispositif names a heterogeneous ensemble of discourses, institutions, laws, and administrative measures with a strategic function. 'Apparatus' (used by most English translators) loses the specifically French legal-administrative connotation (dispositif d'un jugement = operative part of a court ruling). Agamben's intervention popularized the Italian dispositivo, further complicating the English reception

Some Anglophone scholars retain the French term untranslated, arguing that 'apparatus' and 'device' each capture only one dimension: apparatus suggests heaviness and centrality, device suggests lightness and instrumentality, while dispositif names the strategic arrangement that can be either. The untranslated usage signals theoretical allegiance to the French original

Refoulement (Freud's Verdrängung) is standardly rendered as 'repression'. The French re-foulement (re-pushing, pushing back) preserves the spatial-dynamic metaphor more transparently than English 'repression' (pressing back/down). Lacan distinguishes refoulement originaire (primal repression) from refoulement proprement dit, a distinction English marks only by adjective, not by the word's internal structure

Pulsion translates Freud's Trieb. English 'drive' (Strachey's choice over 'instinct') is now standard but lacks the Latin resonance of pulsion (pulsio = pushing). French pulsion clearly differentiates from instinct, while the English 'drive' vs 'instinct' distinction required decades of editorial effort to establish against Strachey's original conflation in the Standard Edition

Désir translates Freud's Wunsch (wish) and Begierde (Hegel, via Kojève). Lacan's désir is not wish-fulfillment but the metonymy of the signifying chain — always désir de l'Autre. English 'desire' is semantically close but misses the Hegelian-Kojèvean layer that French philosophical culture made available to Lacan: désir as the motor of dialectical recognition, not merely wanting

Universally retained in French in Anglophone literature. Lacan himself insisted the term not be translated. The 'a' stands for autre (other, lowercase) as opposed to Autre (Other, uppercase). Any translation ('object small-a', 'object little-a') would lose the algebraic opacity Lacan intended — the letter resists imaginary capture precisely by remaining untranslatable

French sujet carries the double sense of grammatical subject and political subject (one who is subjected to sovereignty) more naturally than English 'subject'. Lacan's sujet barré (barred subject, $) exploits this duality: the subject is both the agent of speech and subjected to the signifying chain. English 'subject' carries both senses but the political-subjection sense is less immediately present

Lacan's Réel is capitalized and opposed to réalité (reality). English capitalizes 'Real' to mark the distinction but cannot reproduce the French réel/réalité opposition within a single morphological family. The Real is what resists symbolization absolutely — English 'real' in everyday usage means the opposite (empirically actual), creating constant interference for non-specialist readers

Lacan's Symbolique (substantivized adjective, le Symbolique) designates the register of language, law, and the signifier. English 'the Symbolic' preserves the substantivization through the definite article. The translation is relatively transparent, though French symbolique carries a trace of the anthropological tradition (Mauss, Lévi-Strauss: échange symbolique) more readily than English 'symbolic'

Lacan's Imaginaire names the register of the image, the ego, and dual relations (stade du miroir). English 'the Imaginary' works but collides with the everyday sense of 'imaginary' (not real, fictitious), which is almost the opposite of Lacan's meaning: the Imaginary is constitutive of subjective experience, not a deficiency of reality-testing

Derrida's déconstruction translates Heidegger's Destruktion/Abbau. The English 'deconstruction' became so widely adopted that it largely replaced the French term in international usage. The translation is morphologically transparent but the English reception detached 'deconstruction' from its Heideggerian genealogy, turning a precise philosophical operation into a loose synonym for critique or dismantling

French trace and English 'trace' are cognates with similar semantic ranges (track, mark, vestige). The translation is unusually transparent. The difficulty lies not in the word itself but in Derrida's technical usage: trace names the archi-écriture (archi-writing) that precedes and conditions both speech and writing — a theoretical weight neither the French nor English everyday word carries

French supplément means both addition (adding to something already complete) and substitution (replacing a lack). Derrida's reading of Rousseau in De la Grammatologie exploits this double logic. English 'supplement' carries both senses etymologically but the substitution-sense is far less active in everyday usage, requiring Derrida's translators to make the duality explicit through commentary

French écriture covers both the act of writing and the broader concept of inscription/script. Derrida's archi-écriture (archi-writing) elevates écriture from an empirical practice to a transcendental condition. English 'writing' works but its strong association with the empirical act of putting pen to paper resists the conceptual elevation Derrida demands

Both French and English borrow from botanical Latin (rhizoma, from Greek rhízōma). The translation is fully transparent. Deleuze-Guattari's metaphorical extension — rhizome as a model of non-hierarchical, multiply-connected thought opposing the arborescent model — transfers intact into English, making this one of the most successful conceptual exports of French theory

Foucault's biopolitique (bio + politique) translates transparently to 'biopolitics'. The morphological structure is preserved. The translation difficulty is not linguistic but conceptual: English 'biopolitics' was subsequently appropriated by Agamben, Esposito, and Hardt/Negri in ways that diverge from Foucault's original usage, making the 'same' English term polysemous in ways the French term's Foucauldian anchoring resists

French discipline and English 'discipline' are cognates with identical double meaning: academic field and bodily/institutional training. Foucault's Surveiller et Punir exploits this duality. The translation is transparent — the problem lies in the book's title: Surveiller et Punir became Discipline and Punish, substituting 'discipline' (a noun from the book's content) for surveiller (to surveil/watch), losing the panoptic gaze that the French title foregrounds

French discours and English 'discourse' are cognates, but Foucault's usage (formation discursive, ordre du discours) gives discours a technical weight absent from the English everyday sense (conversation, discussion). The translation works terminologically but English 'discourse' has been subsequently diluted by its adoption across the humanities as a near-synonym for 'discussion about', far from Foucault's archaeological-genealogical precision

The title Surveiller et Punir was translated as Discipline and Punish, replacing the infinitive surveiller (to watch over, to surveil) with the noun 'discipline'. This is one of the most consequential mistranslations in French theory reception: the French title centers the gaze (the panopticon), while the English title centers the institution. Sheridan's choice prioritized thematic coherence over literal fidelity

In Foucault, savoir designates the epistemological field that makes connaissance (scientific knowledge) possible — L'Archéologie du savoir. English 'knowledge' cannot distinguish savoir from connaissance, collapsing the condition of possibility into the conditioned. 'The Archaeology of Knowledge' is technically about savoir (the ground), not connaissance (the figure), but the English title cannot mark this

Foucault's énoncé is the basic unit of discourse in L'Archéologie du savoir — not a sentence, not a proposition, not a speech act, but the function that makes these possible. English 'statement' (Sheridan's choice) carries connotations of intentional assertion absent from Foucault's usage, where the énoncé is an anonymous, impersonal function of the discursive field

Lacan's l'Autre (capital A, the big Other) designates the symbolic order, the locus of speech. English 'the Other' works but cannot graphically distinguish grand Autre from petit autre as economically as French: the uppercase/lowercase distinction must be explicitly marked in English commentary whereas French readers see it immediately in the article (l'Autre vs l'autre)

Lacan's l'autre (lowercase, the small other/little other) designates the imaginary counterpart, the mirror-image, the semblable. English 'the other' (lowercase) preserves the distinction from 'the Other' (uppercase) but the graphic economy of the French opposition is weakened in English where capitalization rules vary by house style and context
